Article Title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max get Variable Aperture as 'most important' camera feature: What it means for users
Article Text:
Apple iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max

Aperture is the part of a camera most phone users never see

The useful bit is what happens when you take control

It is not just about low light

The aperture is only on one camera

Apple is adding more control to video too

The idea isn't new to smartphones

The bigger camera change is the combination

What variable aperture actually changes for iPhone users

Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control how much light reaches the sensor for the first time on an iPhone.The feature sits alongside a new 48MP Fusion Main camera, a redesigned sensor and new Pro Controls. Apple says the six laser-cut blades inside the lens can move between four aperture settings, while the camera can also adjust the aperture automatically depending on the scene.That sounds like a minor hardware upgrade. But it is not. The lens opening affects exposure, depth of field, and how motion is captured, so giving the iPhone aperture control adds something software alone can't quite duplicate.Apple's description is straightforward: "iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn't possible before," Apple said. "This is the most advanced camera we've ever made."Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. It is measured using f-numbers such as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0.The lower the f-number, the wider the opening and the more light reaches the sensor.A wider aperture can therefore help in darker conditions. A narrower aperture lets in less light, but it also keeps more of the scene in focus.Most smartphone cameras use a fixed aperture. The lens has one opening, and the phone relies heavily on shutter speed, ISO, and computational photography to handle different lighting conditions.The iPhone 18 Pro changes that for its main camera. Its lens can open as wide as f/1.48 and then stop down to f/1.8, f/2.8 or f/4.0. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size.Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.The camera can make that decision automatically. In a darker scene, it can open the aperture to f/1.48 and let in more light. In brighter conditions, it can narrow the opening.For most people, the automatic system will do most of the work. The Camera app can choose an aperture based on the scene, just as it already decides on exposure and other settings.The difference is that iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max owners can also take control themselves.Apple's new Pro Controls let users manually change aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. A histogram can also be displayed to help judge exposure across a scene.That gives photographers another way to decide how a picture should look, instead of leaving every exposure decision to the camera.The most obvious example is depth of field. At a wider aperture such as f/1.48, the camera can produce more optical background blur when the subject is relatively close and the background is farther away.Stopping down to f/4.0 has the opposite effect. More of the scene can stay in focus, which can help with landscapes or group photos where people stand at different distances from the camera.That matters because a group shot can otherwise leave one person sharp while another, standing slightly farther away, falls outside the plane of focus. A narrower aperture gives the camera more room to keep those subjects in focus.It also gives photographers another option when deliberately introducing motion into an image. A narrower aperture reduces the amount of light entering the lens, making it easier to use a slower shutter speed when conditions are bright enough.The obvious benefit of opening the aperture is light. Apple says the main camera can open to ƒ/1.48 for low-light photography, letting more light reach the sensor.That can give the camera more flexibility before it has to compensate by increasing ISO or slowing the shutter speed. In practical terms, that can help preserve detail and reduce noise, while a fast enough shutter can keep moving subjects sharp.But variable aperture is useful in the opposite direction too.In bright daylight, photographers sometimes want a slower shutter speed to create motion blur. That can be useful with moving water, people, or cars, and it also matters in video, where shutter speed is normally tied to frame rate.A fixed wide aperture can make that difficult in strong sunlight because too much light reaches the sensor even when the shutter is already operating at its fastest useful setting. Stopping the lens down gives the camera another way to reduce exposure.There are limits, though. A range ending at f/4.0 does not eliminate the need for neutral-density filters in every bright-light situation. Photographers who want long exposures in direct sunlight may still need an ND filter to cut the light further.Apple's implementation has an important limitation. The variable aperture is on the main 24mm camera. It does not extend across the entire rear camera system.The ultra-wide and telephoto cameras don't have the same variable-aperture mechanism. That means the new optical control is available only when shooting through the main lens.This is also why the feature should not be viewed as a replacement for the other cameras or for computational photography. Exposure, autofocus, HDR, noise reduction and image processing still determine much of the final photograph.The hardware simply gives the camera another physical variable to work with before those processes take over.Aperture changes also feed into Apple's video features. The new Pro Controls work with video as well as photography, letting users manually adjust settings including aperture and shutter speed. That is especially relevant for people who want more predictable exposure rather than letting the phone change settings during recording.Apple has also added the ability to apply Cinematic effects after capture to videos recorded at up to 60 frames per second. That means users can make this adjustment after recording instead of committing to the effect while shooting.Time-lapse recording now supports 4K and Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix has new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.The combination is notable because Apple isn't presenting the variable aperture as an isolated camera specification. It is part of a broader attempt to give users more control over how photos and video are captured and processed.Apple is not the first phone maker to put a variable aperture in a smartphone. Samsung introduced a dual-aperture system with the Galaxy S9 series in 2018. That system switched between f/1.5 and f/2.4 depending on the lighting conditions.Huawei later introduced more flexible variable-aperture systems, while Xiaomi and Honor have also used the technology in flagship phones.The reason it has remained relatively uncommon is fairly simple: fitting a mechanical aperture mechanism into a smartphone camera adds complexity to an already tightly packed module.For years, phone makers instead concentrated on larger sensors, multiple cameras and computational photography. Those technologies can compensate for many of the limitations of a fixed aperture without adding moving parts to the lens.The iPhone 18 Pro's approach is therefore less about replacing computational photography than adding an optical control alongside it.The variable aperture gets most of the attention, but Apple has made several other changes to the camera system.The 48MP Fusion Main camera uses a new sensor and a new computational imaging pipeline that Apple says produces sharper, more detailed images. Photographic Styles now include additional texture and grain controls, giving users more ways to change the look of their photos.Apple has also added persistent subject tracking for photos and video, letting the camera keep following a person even if they temporarily disappear behind someone else in a crowd.Another feature aimed at photographers is Apple Reference Image. When Reference mode is used, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute turns into what Apple describes as an "unalterable reference image." You can then view the reference alongside the main photograph in the Photos app.The idea is to compare the original sensor-derived reference with the photograph and identify whether changes have been made. Apple says the feature is intended to address image authenticity, particularly for photographers and photojournalists.Apple is also adding metadata support and upcoming support for the SynthID standard to help identify images generated or edited with AI.For someone who simply opens the Camera app and takes pictures, it may not change much. The phone can choose the aperture automatically, just as it already handles most exposure decisions. For people who shoot deliberately, the change is more useful.A wider f/1.48 setting can help in darker scenes. Stopping down can keep more of a group or landscape in focus. Manual aperture control can also be combined with shutter-speed control to create particular motion effects.It can even produce optical effects that fixed-aperture smartphone cameras cannot reproduce in the same way, including changes in how bright points of light appear at narrower apertures.But four aperture settings don't turn the iPhone into a dedicated interchangeable-lens camera. The sensor remains small compared with most conventional cameras, and the amount of natural optical background blur depends heavily on the distance between the camera, subject, and background.For many portraits, Apple's computational Portrait mode will still produce a stronger and more controllable background-blur effect.The same is true for long exposures in bright daylight. The f/1.48-to-f/4.0 range gives photographers more room, but it does not remove the physical limits imposed by available light.That is probably the right way to look at the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture. It gives the camera one more physical control over exposure and focus, while the sensor and software continue to determine what ultimately reaches the screen.For casual users, most of that will happen automatically. For photographers and videographers who want to decide how the shot is captured, the four aperture settings and Pro Controls make the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max considerably more flexible than a fixed-aperture iPhone.
Article Summary: Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size. Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.

Article Title: Google unveils five new sustainability initiatives in India
Article Text: Google is expanding its Solar API to cover more than 300 million rooftops in India, enabling faster and more accurate rooftop solar assessments. Installers can now evaluate a home’s solar potential without an on‑site visit, reducing time and cost. Platforms like Solar Ladder and OpenSolar have already integrated Solar API insights to streamline proposal creation and automate manual roof surveys.Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. The company will receive environmental attributes from the clean electricity generated, helping address electricity‑related emissions across its value chain. This marks Google’s second Scope 3‑focused solar project in India, bringing total added capacity to 300 MW.Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate‑smart farming method that reduces methane emissions and conserves water. The initiative is expected to generate up to 3 million tonnes of CO₂e in near‑term warming impact (GWP20) and conserve billions of gallons of water.NASA‑enabled satellite verification will support monitoring and farmer adoption.The Google Center for Climate Technology has selected three inaugural projects focused on green workforce training and low‑carbon construction materials. Google is adding two new focus areas—water stewardship and waste & circularity—and is inviting proposals via the Manthan Platform. Selected applicants will receive support to develop scalable, data‑driven environmental solutions.Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet, featuring four Indian startups: Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests, and Climitra Carbon. These companies use AI, Geo‑AI, drones and satellite models to empower farmers, scale agroforestry, restore biodiversity, and convert biomass into biochar.These five initiatives reflect Google’s push to combine AI, research partnerships and local innovation to advance sustainable development and climate resilience across India.
Article Summary: Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt a climate‑smart farming method. Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet.

Article Title: 1980s AI Photo trend: 5 ChatGPT prompts to create Kerala-style retro images

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: By 2008, New Hampshire researchers had tested porous asphalt through four winters; a later study found it could cut annual salt use by 64% to 77%
Article Text:
AI Representation: Porous asphalt lets winter meltwater drain through the pavement. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 2004-to-2008 UNH parking lot study tracked porous asphalt through four winters

Faster snowmelt and less ice buildup reduced how often crews needed to plow or salt

A follow-up 2014 study quantified the salt savings across two adjacent test lots

Engineers approach pavement design in cold climates. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The findings pointed toward a practical case for reduced-salt winter maintenance

UNH researchers conducted a study from 2004 through 2008 involving a porous asphalt parking lot in Durham that examined how well the quicker drainage and increased friction properties performed during multiple winter seasons in New England, as explained in a report from the UNH Stormwater Center detailing the results. In a subsequent study of the exact same site, researchers determined how much salt could be saved using the porous asphalt surface, which was about 75% per year without sacrificing safety.The first study, Water Quality and Hydrologic Performance of a Porous Asphalt Pavement as a Storm-Water Treatment Strategy in a Cold Climate, published in the Journal of Environmental Engineering in 2012, reports that the pavement's infiltration capacity ranged from about 1,490 to 2,690 cm/h even after repeated freeze-thaw cycles, despite maximum frost penetration reaching nearly 71 cm. It also found exceptional water-quality treatment performance for pollutants like petroleum hydrocarbons, zinc, and suspended solids, with no consistent seasonal decline over the four winters monitored, and with frost impacts limited by the well-drained stone reservoir beneath the surface. The system retained or infiltrated a substantial share of incoming precipitation across the monitoring period, with no seasonal drop-off in that performance, evidence that the drainage benefit persisted well beyond the warmer months.The meltwater passes through the surface rather than remaining on top, so porous asphalt surfaces accumulate fewer amounts of snow, slush and ice compared to normal dense-mix surfaces under similar treatments. In the field tests conducted, the porous surface had been observed to be comparatively cleaner and drier one hour after plowing, owing to the open-graded design of the pavement material, which removes moisture from the surface. Fewer amounts of ice formations on the surface allowed the surface to maintain its skid resistance on its own without relying on frequent applications of salts. The skid resistance measured using a British pendulum tester, yielding the British pendulum number, remained high on the porous asphalt surface even with the reduction of salt application.The second study, Assessment of Winter Maintenance of Porous Asphalt and Its Function for Chloride Source Control, published in the Journal of Transportation Engineering in 2014 (Roseen, Ballestero, Houle, Heath, and Houle), found that the porous asphalt achieved similar or better surface conditions using 64 to 77 percent less salt than the dense-mix reference surface, even though the dense-mix lot received a standard salting rate roughly four times higher, by design, as the conventional-maintenance comparison point.The earlier research mentioned this because it took a considerably lower quantity of salt to make the porous surface equally safe. The calculations made in 2014 showed that the reduction was 64-77%, which is an average of 75% less salt used per year, while the friction on the surface of porous asphalt was equal to or even higher than on the conventional one. There were instances when the porous surface, despite not being salted at all, had better performance results than the conventional one, even if it was fully salted.The roughly 75 percent reduction in salt use is valuable for more than just maintenance budgets: road salt is a well-documented source of chloride pollution in groundwater and surface waters, so less salt applied means less chloride released into those waters in the first place. The findings of the tests of the porous asphalt mentioned above suggest that it is the pavement design itself, not the change in salting technology or equipment, that leads to such results.Taken together, the two UNH studies suggest sustained drainage performance over time and show a substantial, if lot-specific, reduction in salt use with this pavement. However, there are some caveats involved. The data for the salt reductions have been lot-specific, depending upon the amount of shade in each lot and the condition in which the stone reservoir underneath has been maintained over time, because clogging caused by sediments and organic matter will cause reductions in the infiltration capacity of the pavement. Nonetheless, the New Hampshire studies still represent one of the most comprehensive long-term datasets concerning the winter performance of porous asphalt.
Article Summary: Porous asphalt lets winter meltwater drain through the pavement. A 2004-to-2008 UNH parking lot study tracked porous asphalt through four winters. Faster snowmelt and less ice buildup reduced how often crews needed to plow or salt.

Article Title: In Gateshead, water trapped 150 metres below the city in abandoned coal mines now heats 350 homes and public buildings

Mine water heat pump powers Gateshead buildings

Why does mine water get warmer with depth

What is the Gateshead living laboratory studying

Water trapped around 150 metres beneath Gateshead is now being used to heat homes and public buildings through a 6-megawatt water-source heat pump. The system, which began operating in March 2023 after three years of development, draws heat from former coal mine workings and sends it through more than 5 kilometres of district heating pipes. It currently serves buildings including Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, offices and 350 council-owned homes. Plans include connecting another 270 privately owned homes, a conference centre and hotel. The project also provides researchers with data on how abandoned mine workings can support lower-carbon heating.A 6 megawatt water-source heat pump recovers heat from the mine water and transfers it into the district heating network. The heated water is then distributed through more than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes to connected buildings.The network currently supplies heat to several types of buildings across Gateshead. These include Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes. The source states that the system is also planned to serve another 270 privately owned homes, as well as a new conference centre and a hotel development.Mine water becomes warmer with increasing depth because of what the Mining Remediation Authority describes as a ‘geothermal gradient’. Mine water temperatures generally range from 10°C to 20°C, although they can reach 40°C at depths of around 1 kilometre. Water can be brought to the surface through boreholes, shafts or adits, before heat exchangers and pumps recover its heat. The authority says mine water temperatures are not affected by seasonal variations. It describes mine water as a potential source of “renewable, secure, low carbon heating for buildings in coalfield areas”, with the right support and sustainable management.The Gateshead mine water heating network is part of a wider research project known as the Gateshead Living Laboratory. The initiative is designed to collect evidence that supports future licensing, management and wider use of mine water heat schemes. It is located near three mine water heat schemes in the North East of England.With support from Gateshead Council, researchers drilled four boreholes and installed monitoring equipment to gather data. The information is available as open-access data for researchers, regulators, stakeholders and academic institutions. The government says the work will help researchers study the thermal and hydrogeological interactions between multiple mine water heat schemes in the Walker mining block in Tyne and Wear.

Article Title: Spanish cave remains reveal repeated cannibalism in prehistoric Europe, from violent deaths to human skulls turned into cups
Article Text:
Image: Cut marks on adult human skull from Majolicas Cave/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Ancient Spanish caves preserve evidence of repeated cannibalism

Cannibalism appeared during several distinct prehistoric periods

Some remains reveal possible episodes of prehistoric violence

Human skulls were transformed into objects after death

Ancient human remains from three caves in southern Spain are revealing a disturbing but complex chapter in Europe’s prehistoric past. Researchers examined nearly 1,000 human bones from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majolicas caves in Granada, finding evidence that people cut, fractured, chewed and deliberately modified human remains during different periods of the Neolithic. The findings suggest cannibalism was not one continuous tradition, but a practice that appeared repeatedly in different contexts over thousands of years, offering clues about prehistoric violence, death and ritual.The remains come from three caves in Granada that have provided archaeologists with evidence of prehistoric human activity for decades. Researchers in ' Multiphase human cannibalism in Neolithic southern Iberia: Chronological and taphonomic evidence from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela, and Majolicas Caves ,' published in Journal of Archaeological Science examined the bones for microscopic traces including cut marks, fractures, impact damage and tooth marks, while also studying how and when the damage occurred. Their analysis found evidence consistent with deliberate processing of human remains at all three sites, although the circumstances varied considerably. At Malalmuerzo, some remains appear connected with violent deaths, while Carigüela contained deliberately modified human skulls. At Majolicas, the treatment of human remains appears to have had a different cultural context, showing that the discovery cannot be reduced to one explanation for prehistoric cannibalism.Rather than suggesting that Neolithic Europeans regularly consumed human flesh, the evidence indicates several separate episodes spread across thousands of years. The researchers identified concentrations around the end of the sixth millennium BC, the middle of the fifth millennium BC and the end of the third millennium BC. At Carigüela, evidence indicates several episodes of cannibalism during the Neolithic, including the deliberate modification of two human skulls into cup-like objects. At Majolicas, the most recent evidence dates to approximately 3800 BC. The pattern suggests that cannibalism repeatedly emerged under particular circumstances rather than representing a permanent or universal feature of prehistoric communities.One of the most striking sets of evidence comes from Malalmuerzo, where fractures and other damage to the bones indicate that some individuals may have died violently. The remains belonged to people of different ages, leading researchers to consider whether a group could have been attacked, killed and subsequently consumed. This interpretation potentially connects cannibalism with conflict between prehistoric communities. However, the researchers do not treat every damaged bone as proof of warfare. The contrasting evidence from the three caves demonstrates that human remains could be processed in different ways and for different reasons, including possible conflict, consumption and cultural or ritual practices.The discoveries at Carigüela offer some of the clearest evidence that the treatment of human remains was not necessarily motivated by hunger alone. Two skulls were deliberately modified into cups, suggesting that parts of the human body could acquire a new symbolic or practical purpose after death. The researchers therefore argue against viewing “Neolithic cannibalism” as one uniform practice. Similar marks on human bones can emerge from very different circumstances, and the archaeological record points towards a complicated relationship between death, the body and community life. These recurring episodes provide a rare glimpse into how prehistoric societies dealt with violence, the dead and relationships between groups.
Article Summary: Researchers examined nearly 1,000 human bones from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majolicas caves in Granada. They found evidence that people cut, fractured, chewed and deliberately modified human remains during different periods of the Neolithic. The findings suggest cannibalism was not one continuous tradition, but a practice that appeared repeatedly over thousands of years.

Article Title: Spain released wild horses into the Iberian Highlands after a 10,000-year absence; the animals are being used to rebuild a fire-prone landscape
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Spain’s wild horses rebuild a fire-prone landscape

Wild horses create a natural firebreak

Image AI generated

Wild horses expand large-herbivore grazing in Spain

Przewalski’s horses are roaming Spain’s Iberian Highlands again after an absence of more than 10,000 years, as a rewilding project uses the animals’ natural grazing to reshape a landscape increasingly vulnerable to wildfires. The horses were released in Villanueva de Alcorón, Guadalajara province, as part of an effort by Rewilding Spain to restore the ecological role once played by large wild herbivores. Their grazing and trampling reduce vegetation and forest biomass, while helping create a more varied landscape of woodland and open pasture. The return of the horses follows their near-extinction in the 20th century and represents a new stage in efforts to restore natural processes across the Iberian Highlands. According to Rewilding Spain, an environmental conservation initiative, the animals can help improve pasture quality and support biodiversity, while reducing the amount of combustible vegetation. The project is an opportunity for visitors to observe horses living freely in Western Europe.Their presence could also benefit insects, birds and smaller mammals by creating patches of shorter grass and disturbed ground.Conservationists will monitor the herd’s health, movements and impact on vegetation, using the results to assess whether similar rewilding approaches could work elsewhere.The horses are not being released simply to increase the number of wild animals in the region. Their grazing is intended to replace an ecological function that was lost after extensive livestock farming, with horses and cattle disappearing from parts of the Alto Tajo. As the animals feed and move through the landscape, they reduce vegetation and forest biomass while creating more varied pasture conditions.Rewilding Spain says natural grazing by large herbivores is important for restoring healthy ecosystems because feeding and trampling can reduce the amount of forest biomass available. The organisation states that the horses “reduce forest biomass available in the area”, while their grazing also improves the diversity and quality of pastures used by deer, roe deer, fallow deer and domestic sheep and goats.The Iberian Highlands have extensive areas of forest and vegetation where a lack of large grazers can allow shrubs and other plants to become denser. Rewilding Spain is using natural grazing as one way of changing that vegetation structure. By eating grasses, shrubs and other plants and moving through the landscape, the horses help create more open areas and a mixture of different vegetation types.The wider rewilding initiative explicitly links this work with wildfire prevention. Horses can help make landscapes more heterogeneous and richer in terms of biodiversity, which it considers important for reducing vulnerability to wildfires. Its Iberian Highlands programme also says horses are helping to open up areas affected by past fires, increasing structural diversity and creating a landscape mosaic that can support regeneration.The return of Przewalski’s horses is also part of a wider programme to restore large-herbivore grazing across the Iberian Highlands. Rewilding Spain is working with Przewalski’s horses alongside Serrano and Pottoka horses and tauros cattle in different parts of the landscape. The organisation says the combined management of large herbivores now covers tens of thousands of hectares, to support forest regeneration, biodiversity and wildfire prevention.The horses are also becoming part of the region’s nature-tourism economy. Their presence has already attracted visitors to Villanueva de Alcorón, where guided trips allow people to see the animals living independently in the landscape.
Article Summary: The horses were released in Villanueva de Alcorón, Guadalajara province, as part of an effort by Rewilding Spain to restore the ecological role once played by large wild herbivores. As the animals feed and move through the landscape, they reduce vegetation and forest biomass while creating more varied pasture conditions.

Article Title: Denmark planted trees for carbon storage, but 21 years later natural forests proved more diverse while plantations captured carbon faster
Article Text:
Image: Canva

What did scientists discover in Denmark after 21 years

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster?

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster? (Image: Canva)

Why were naturally regenerated forests more diverse?

What does the research mean for future forest restoration?

Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21 years, scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures. The University of Copenhagen conducted a rare long-term comparison of two approaches to forest restoration and found why future reforestation projects may need to balance rapid carbon capture with biodiversity recovery and ecological complexity.The study ‘ Passive versus active afforestation of agricultural land: Two decades of impacts on tree biomass and ecosystem carbon storage ’ compared agricultural land that had been abandoned and allowed to regenerate naturally with areas that had been actively planted to create plantation forests. After approximately 21 years, clear differences had emerged between the two approaches. Plantation forests had accumulated substantially more tree biomass than naturally colonised forests, demonstrating that deliberate planting can accelerate early forest development and carbon storage.Naturally regenerated areas, however, developed a different ecological character as vegetation colonised the abandoned farmland without the same intensive planting approach. The researchers also compared these younger forests with mature, actively managed forests, providing a longer-term reference point. The findings show that forest recovery cannot be judged by carbon storage alone.The plantations had the advantage of being able to accumulate more biomass early in their life due to trees being purposefully planted instead of waiting for them to come naturally as part of the process of succession. This study shows that the plantation forests have 16 times more above-ground woody biomass compared to the naturally colonised forests within a period of about twenty years. As such, the faster accumulation of biomass led to faster accumulation of carbon in the trees within the early stage of forest development. It is important to note that fast biomass accumulation does not necessarily mean that the plantation mimics all the ecological features of a mature forest.The colonisation that occurred naturally enabled vegetation to grow by the means of ecological succession without any predetermined planting. This process will take more time, but will lead to greater diversity of plants in terms of their species and structure since different plants will colonise certain areas. The Danish study showed that the naturally colonised forests were distinct from the plantation in terms of vegetation and ecology, which proves the necessity of using natural factors in the process of creation of the forest. However, this statement does not mean that plantations cannot be valuable in terms of biodiversity, but only that the structure and composition of such forests differ greatly from the forests developed without planting.The results imply that there is no one particular forest restoration approach that would optimise all of the environmental benefits at once. Plantations would be an advantageous choice if the aim is to achieve rapid carbon sequestration because plantations would help to achieve faster carbon accumulation. As for natural regeneration, it would provide greater ecological diversity as the forest develops and could contribute significantly to biodiversity. Therefore, the scientists show a more complex view of afforestation that does not include only the number of trees planted.
Article Summary: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. Scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures.

Article Title: Copenhagen’s £200m underground Natural History Museum, under construction since 2019, to open in 2027 with eight galleries, 14m specimens, dinosaur skeletons, 3D exhibits and Ocean Hall
Article Text:
Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Eight galleries will be built underground

The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

The museum’s collection includes around 14 million specimens gathered over 400 years. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

14 million specimens include dinosaur skeletons

Interactive 3D exhibits will allow visitors to explore detailed digital scans of specimens. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Ocean Hall features a huge glass dome

The spectacular Ocean Hall will feature a huge dome made with 1,600 triangular glass panels. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

£200 million project has taken years to complete

Museum will sit alongside Copenhagen’s Botanical Garden

A huge new underground attraction is set to open in one of Europe’s most popular cities, promising visitors immersive experiences, dinosaur fossils and access to millions of specimens collected over centuries.The new Natural History Museum in Copenhagen, Denmark, will officially open on March 6, 2027, following a major £200 million redevelopment project that has been years in the making.The centrepiece of the project is a series of eight new galleries built underground, creating a vast new exhibition space beneath Copenhagen’s historic Botanical Garden.The eight exhibitions will be titled Universe, Earth, Life, Denmark, Arctic, Biodiversity, Humans and Ocean Hall, taking visitors on a journey through the history of the natural world, according to The Official Copenhagen City Card website.The museum has been designed to combine Copenhagen’s historic architecture with a striking new underground complex.According to architect Lene Tranberg, natural light will reach the underground exhibition galleries through skylights, while the design aims to “engage all the senses”.Inside, visitors will find concrete interiors, curved staircases and large exhibition spaces designed to create an immersive journey through natural history.The new museum connects the Botanical Garden, the existing historic buildings and new architecture inspired by organic forms found in nature.The museum says the project represents a new direction in Danish museum architecture, combining protected historic surroundings with new underground galleries and above-ground structures inspired by nature.The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including fossils and specimens documenting the history and diversity of life on Earth.Among the highlights are dinosaur remains, including a 17-metre-long Diplodocus skeleton and T-Rex skeletons.Visitors will also be able to explore specimens using interactive touchscreen tables, allowing them to rotate and zoom into 3D scans of objects from the museum's collections.The exhibitions will cover everything from the formation of the Solar System and the origins of species to biodiversity and the rapidly changing natural world.The scale of the new museum can be seen in the construction details.The exhibition halls have walls reaching up to 10 metres high, while ceilings are made using around 180,000 small wooden slats, designed to improve acoustics across the large spaces.The Ocean Hall measures 16 metres wide, 23 metres high and 50 metres long. Its dome consists of 2,000 steel frames fitted with 1,600 triangular glass panels.Remarkably, only two of the glass panes in the entire structure are identical.The museum's welcome hall is housed in a former engine house that was dismantled and reconstructed using original facade bricks and steel lattice structures.The excavation for the foundations reached 15 metres deep and stretched 400 metres in circumference.Plans for the new museum were first revealed around 17 years ago, while construction began in 2019.The project was originally expected to open much earlier, but planning permission and funding issues contributed to significant delays.The exhibition concept was developed by the museum in collaboration with design agency Tinker Imagineers, which won an international competition in 2018. In 2023, the project entered its production phase, with Event Communications winning the contract to deliver the new permanent exhibitions.Christine Wiberg-Lyng, Foundation Director at Aage og Johanne Louis-Hansens Fond, said the new buildings create a sensory setting that supports the museum's core purpose.The redevelopment will add around 7,000 square metres of exhibition space, while another 2,000 square metres will include public facilities such as the shop, ticket office, VILLUM Hall, restaurant, café and dining areas.Around 500 square metres will be dedicated to teaching facilities for school students.Collection storage, laboratories, offices and other staff facilities will occupy approximately 22,500 square metres. Overall, the new museum will comprise around 32,000 square metres, divided almost equally between new construction and renovated historic buildings.Above the underground galleries, Copenhagen's Botanical Garden offers visitors a living museum containing around 13,000 plant species, alongside alpine rock gardens and walking trails.The site also includes the Palm House and Butterfly House, located inside a Victorian cast-iron glasshouse dating back to 1874.The Botanical Garden is free to enter, while tickets for the new museum are listed at approximately £13.22 for adults and £5.75 for children aged three to 17.
Article Summary: Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including dinosaur remains.

Article Title: China planted three types of forests on the Loess Plateau; 18 years later, natural forests held 8% more soil moisture
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Natural forests held 8% more soil moisture

How did natural forests improve soil water storage

Image AI generated

Why did natural forests retain more soil moisture

China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to regenerate naturally. Researchers spent 18 years monitoring four forest types in the region, comparing plantations of Pinus tabuliformis, Platycladus orientalis and Robinia pseudoacacia with a natural secondary forest. The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests, while recording greater macroporosity and stronger water movement through the soil. Its soil held more water after rainfall, with average soil water storage reaching around 6 mm, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. Over the 2006–2024 monitoring period, the natural forest consistently maintained higher soil water content, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining moisture trends. The researchers also found that natural forest soils had lower bulk density and higher levels of soil organic carbon and total nitrogen.These differences suggest that allowing forests to recover naturally may improve the soil’s ability to absorb and retain rainfall. The findings could help guide restoration across water-limited landscapes, where choosing suitable forest types is important for balancing vegetation recovery with available water resources.According to the study published in Water Resources Research, titled ‘Natural Forests Accelerate Soil Hydrological Processes and Enhance Water-Holding Capacities Compared to Planted Forests After Long-Term Restoration ’, natural secondary forests had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests. They also had 68.7% greater macroporosity, a 13.7% larger mean equivalent pore diameter and 34.2% higher saturated hydraulic conductivity. The researchers also recorded higher soil organic carbon, field capacity and available water content in the natural forests.The difference was also visible across the 18-year monitoring period. Natural secondary forests consistently maintained higher soil water content, with peak values reaching 0.28 cm³ per cm³, particularly after substantial rainfall. Pinus tabuliformis showed a slight increase in soil moisture over the period, reaching 0.24 cm³ per cm³, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining soil moisture trends, with average values between 0.15 and 0.22 cm³ per cm³.The researchers found clear differences in soil structure between the forests. Natural secondary forest soils had the highest macroporosity and better-connected pores. Their mean macroporosity was 0.113 mm³ per mm³, compared with 0.089 for Robinia pseudoacacia, 0.065 for Platycladus orientalis and 0.047 for Pinus tabuliformis.The natural forests also showed faster soil-water processes during rainfall. Average soil water storage was around 6 mm in the secondary forests, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. The researchers linked this greater storage to the natural forests’ higher macroporosity and pore connectivity, which allowed rainfall to be redistributed and infiltrate the soil more efficiently.Soil moisture in Pinus tabuliformis and Robinia pseudoacacia dropped substantially during the driest period from June to August. In the upper 60 cm of soil, moisture fell. Platycladus orientalis retained more water in deeper layers, but moisture still declined in the upper soil. The secondary forest maintained higher and more stable moisture, particularly in the upper 60 cm.The researchers also found that the secondary forest had lower bulk density, at about 1.0 g per cm³, in the three planted forests. Its soils also contained generally higher levels of total nitrogen and soil organic carbon. The study’s analysis identified soil properties such as bulk density and organic carbon, together with understory plant diversity, as important factors associated with soil hydrological processes and water-holding capacity.
Article Summary: China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to regenerate naturally. Researchers spent 18 years monitoring four forest types in the region, comparing plantations of Pinus tabuliformis, Platycladus orientalis and Robinia pseudoacacia. The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests.

Article Title: In 1978, Massachusetts dumped concrete-filled tyres into the ocean; decades later, they had become a thriving habitat for marine life
Article Text:
Massachusetts built its first permitted artificial reef with concrete-filled tyres

The underwater structures showed little sign of drifting away

The 2019 survey revealed how quickly fish found the reef

The tyre bundles created shelter and surfaces for marine life

New structures continued to reshape the Yarmouth reef

A pile of concrete-filled tyres may not look like much from above, but beneath the surface it can become something very different. Off Yarmouth, Massachusetts, the unusual structures form part of an artificial reef that has been developing in Nantucket Sound since 1978. The project was designed to introduce physical complexity to a sandy seabed and provide habitat for fish and lobsters. Over time, the reef expanded to roughly 2,500 original units across 127 acres, while later additions brought in concrete and granite. Surveys in 2019 gave researchers another way to measure its effect, revealing a striking difference in how quickly fish reached structured reef habitat and bare sand.The Yarmouth reef was developed by the town's Department of Natural Resources with assistance from the Division of Marine Fisheries. It became the first permitted artificial reef of its kind in Massachusetts and was positioned more than two miles south of the mouth of Bass River.The original units were relatively simple. Three to five tyres were filled with concrete and fastened together in bundles, creating a low structure above the seabed.About 1,500 units went into the water in 1978, followed by another 1,000 in 1994, bringing the total to roughly 2,500. The aim was to introduce physical complexity into an otherwise relatively featureless stretch of bottom, giving fish and lobsters places to shelter and move around.Massachusetts' artificial reef programme describes such structures as deliberately placed habitat for fish, with potential benefits for fisheries and recreational fishing.Surveys conducted by the Division of Marine Fisheries in 2009 and 2010 used side-scan sonar and divers to examine the site. They found little evidence of reef material moving outside the permitted area. The northern part of the site contained the highest concentration of deployed material, while fish numbers were also higher where more reef structure was present. Scup and black sea bass were among the fish found in substantial numbers.The structures were being managed as habitat. The Massachusetts artificial reef programme uses surveys, diving and remote sensing to track how these sites perform and how marine communities develop around them.In a 2019 survey, researchers compared the Yarmouth reef with another artificial reef, a natural reef and an area of relatively featureless bottom. Underwater video cameras were used to observe fish arriving at the different sites.The contrast was striking in terms of arrival time, without needing a dramatic interpretation. Finfish appeared on camera after an average of about 33 seconds at reef sites, compared with 502 seconds at the bare control. That is roughly eight minutes and 22 seconds over the unstructured seabed. The study calculated that fish appeared on reef sites 93.4% faster than at the bare control.The result did not mean every reef was identical. The study also measured species richness and diversity at Yarmouth, Harwich, a natural reef and the bare control. Black sea bass and scup were among the species recorded across the sites, while the researchers found differences in the composition of fish communities depending on the location and reef age.The value of an artificial reef comes partly from the spaces created around and between its structures. A flat sandy bottom offers relatively little vertical relief. Bundled structures create edges, gaps and surfaces where animals can shelter, feed or attach themselves.The Yarmouth site has been associated with a range of marine life, including black sea bass, scup, tautog, summer flounder, winter flounder and lobsters. Other species recorded on the reef include blue mussels, cunner, butterfish, longfin squid and knobbed whelk.The reef therefore became more than a collection of objects placed underwater. Over time, marine organisms colonised the available surfaces, while fish used the added structure as part of the surrounding habitat. Massachusetts' artificial reef planning documents describe earlier monitoring at Yarmouth as showing stabilisation of the structures, colonisation by marine organisms and increased recreational fishing activity.The original 1978 deployment was not the end of the project. In 2014, the town and the Division of Marine Fisheries received permits to add further reef material in parts of the site where surveys had identified lower concentrations of existing structures.More material was added again around 2019 and early 2020. This included retired concrete buoy sinkers from the US Coast Guard, granite blocks recovered from demolition projects and other concrete material. More than 3,000 cubic yards of new material were involved across the two deployment efforts.The later additions also changed the character of the reef. Rather than relying only on the original tyre bundles, the site began incorporating approved construction and infrastructure materials that could provide similar physical relief. A Massachusetts habitat-enhancement project, for example, used more than 2,200 cubic yards of material to create additional structured habitat within an undeveloped part of the permitted reef area.
Article Summary: Massachusetts built its first permitted artificial reef with concrete-filled tyres in 1978. The project was designed to introduce physical complexity to a sandy seabed and provide habitat for fish and lobsters. Over time, the reef expanded to roughly 2,500 original units across 127 acres.

Article Title: Meet Eric Thompson, the 39-year-old Texas engineer who has collected 5,000 condiment packets, including nearly 400 Taco Bell designs and a toothpaste sachet from 1950
Article Text:
Eric Thompson's collection spans ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, relish, barbecue sauce, honey, jelly, seafood sauces, vinegar and numerous Asian condiments.

From a college rainbow to a serious archive

Cleaning, cataloging and preserving every packet

Preserving everyday Americana

Most people tear open a condiment packet, squeeze out the last drop and toss the wrapper without a second thought. Eric Thompson sees something beyond: a tiny piece of design, advertising and everyday history. Across his Texas home, thousands of these disposable packets have been transformed from fast-food leftovers into a meticulously organized archive. Meet Eric, a 39-year-old computer engineer from Helotes who has amassed roughly 5,000 single-serving sauce packets, turning an ordinary dining accessory into an unusually detailed collecting hobby.According to a report by the San Antonio Express-News, Thompson's collection spans ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, relish, barbecue sauce, honey, jelly, seafood sauces, vinegar and numerous Asian condiments. Even Whataburger's small, box-shaped ketchup tubs have earned a place in the archive. Around 3,100 individual designs have been cataloged in his online Condiment Packet Archive, where packets are organized by brand, color, date and flavor. His collection also appears on TikTok, where he shares discoveries and the stories behind unusual designs. Hot sauce is the largest category, with about 760 designs. Taco Bell is the standout brand, accounting for nearly 400 distinct packets.The chain's wide range of sauces and frequent use of humorous packaging have made its packets particularly collectible.As per the same online report, Thompson's fascination began in 2007 while he was studying at Penn State. A colorful arrangement of condiment packets caught his attention, creating what looked like a miniature rainbow across a communal food area. When the arrangement later disappeared after a vendor change, Thompson saved several of the remaining packets. What began as an appreciation for the visual arrangement gradually developed into an interest in documenting the evolution of condiment packaging. Today, he tries to collect at least three copies of each new design. One becomes part of the archive, while additional examples can be kept for trading or preservation.The process is considerably more involved than simply picking up discarded wrappers. Thompson carefully opens each packet, empties the contents—often using them with his meals—and then washes and dries the packaging. Once clean, the packet is cataloged and placed inside a protective plastic sleeve similar to those used for trading cards. The sleeves are organized in color-coded containers, although hundreds of packets remain in the queue awaiting processing. Thompson estimates he averages about five packets a night. The collection includes several hundred vintage examples from the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s. Its oldest item is particularly unusual: a squeezable Fuller Brush Company toothpaste packet dating to 1950.Tiny packages with a big historyThe collection also provides a window into how companies use color, typography and packaging to communicate with consumers. Red commonly signals ketchup, while yellow suggests mustard, creating visual expectations before a packet is even opened. Thompson is particularly interested in designs that break those conventions, including unusual colors and generic packaging that reveal different approaches to branding. His Heinz collection alone contains 309 different packets from the United States, Europe and the United Kingdom. Rare finds also turn up through online marketplaces and donations from collectors around the world.Thompson's collection has now earned a place in Ripley's Believe It or Not! Wired into Weird, the franchise's 23rd annual collection of unusual people and discoveries. What makes the archive remarkable is not simply its size. These tiny two-by-three-inch packages document changing tastes, advertising styles, restaurant culture and consumer habits. Something designed to be used for seconds can therefore survive for decades—not because it was meant to be preserved, but because one collector recognized that even the most disposable objects can carry a story.Images Courtesy: San Antonio Express-News

His collection spans ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, relish, barbecue sauce, honey, jelly, seafood sauces, vinegar and numerous Asian condiments. Around 3,100 individual designs have been cataloged in his online Condiment Packet Archive. Thompson estimates he averages about five packets a night.

On the outside, oyster shells collected from a local restaurant were turned into experimental tiles designed to protect that insulation from the weather. Some shells were used directly, while others were heated at around 900°C to make quicklime before being combined with crushed shell. The mixture was moulded and left to harden, producing tiles that became part of the building's exterior. By using discarded bedding and oyster shells, the project tested whether everyday waste could serve a useful purpose while reducing the demand for conventional building materials.The University of Brighton team developed the tiles as part of a project exploring how waste materials could be reused in construction. The tiles were designed to remain on the outer surface of the Brighton Waste House, protecting insulation made from reused bedding and duvets. The project brought together the university team and Local Works Studio, a specialist working on material development. The oyster shells came from English’s restaurant in Brighton, which supplied shells that would otherwise have been discarded. Construction waste from the Preston Barracks development was also incorporated into the project, bringing together two different waste streams to create a new building material.Some were used directly, while others were heated to create quick lime. The project record describes shells being burnt at about 900 degrees before being combined with crushed oyster shells, which acted as aggregate. The mixture was then pressed into silicone moulds and left for several days. After adding water, the mixture underwent a natural chemical reaction that made it hard. As part of the INTERREG SB&WRC programme, researchers explored whether waste materials found near construction sites could be reused for insulation and rain-screen external wall coverings in social housing. Samples were exhibited in Adelaide, South Australia, in 2018 as part of an exhibition linked to the ‘Unmaking Waste conference’. The event brought attention to the project’s attempt to connect waste, design and construction through a prototype. The Brighton work was led by Duncan Baker-Brown with Nick Gant, alongside collaborators including Local Works Studio. Article Title: A Newport mansion is being restored with a staircase technique dating to the 1500s; instead of modern exposed fasteners, craftsmen lock the wooden steps together with mortises and wedges
Article Text:
The project’s heart is a dramatic helical staircase with laminated curved stringers and mortised-and-wedged treads and risers. As per reports, the technique originated in the construction of European staircases in the late 1500s, when wealthy homes and castles had elaborate staircases.

A 16th-century technique finds a modern revival

Made to move with the building

Old craftsmanship comes back with technology

A full-scale rehearsal workshop

A stairway goes up to nowhere in a woodshop. No grand foyer at the bottom, no upper floor waiting at the top—just a full-scale helical structure surrounded by tools, machinery, and carefully prepared pieces of wood. But this unfinished staircase is also something much more: an intersection of centuries-old craftsmanship and contemporary engineering. Wondering what it is? Well, there is a stairway being built for the restoration of a historic home in Newport, Rhode Island. It is a Mark Richey Woodworking’s design and a revival of a late 16th century European method of building stairs, and uses modern computer modeling and manufacturing technology to achieve accurate results. According to an online report by Markrichey website, Newport is known for its grand Gilded Age homes, famously and somewhat facetiously referred to as “summer cottages.” Buildings like The Breakers, Miramar and Hammersmith Farm helped make the city a showcase of American architectural history. And this private residence being restored has undergone many renovations over the years. The current owners wanted to modernize the property but keep the character and craftsmanship that was part of the original design, states the online report.This went beyond just copying an old-fashioned look, as the architectural team also wanted construction techniques that would allow for the durability, precision and visual cleanliness of historic restoration. And that is when Mark Richey Woodworking was brought onto the project for its architectural millwork expertise and its knowledge of traditional woodworking methods.The project’s heart is a dramatic helical staircase with laminated curved stringers and mortised-and-wedged treads and risers. As per reports, the technique originated in the construction of European staircases in the late 1500s, when wealthy homes and castles had elaborate staircases. This method does not use visible screws or nails to hold the finished treads and risers like many modern site-built stairs. Instead, each tread fits into a precisely cut recess—a mortise—and wooden wedges, glued in place on either side in the stringers, hold the components together. The result is a self-securing structure, each tread/riser assembly provides stability for the next. A hidden connection can also be used from below at the tongue and groove joint, but the finished walking surfaces are free of exposed fasteners.Historic buildings with wood framing are especially problematic, as they are never truly static. Wood expands and contracts with the seasons. Buildings settle, framing can shift over time. Face-fastened treads on notched stringers are common in conventional stairs and can cause gaps, squeaks and the look of filled screw or nail holes as these movements occur. The installation can be more difficult because the individual pieces often require a lot of fitting on the construction site. Another way to go is mortised-and-wedged construction. The technique aims to keep the joints tight by mechanically locking the wooden components together and to produce a strong, rigid assembly that can span considerable distances without additional support. The method offers both structural and esthetic benefits for a historic residence where appearance and longevity are equally important.The staircase is built in an old way of construction, but its creation is based on modern technology. Mark Richey Woodworking works with architects and builders during the design phase, helping to translate lofty architectural visions into components that can be manufactured. Engineers model complex shapes on 3D CAD systems and can check the design before starting fabrication. As per the online report, computer-controlled machinery produces components with the accuracy required for complex joinery, while skilled craftsmen do the fitting, laminating and finishing. This mix also reduces uncertainty at time of installation. The workshop can provide the staircase as a carefully engineered kit of parts, rather than shipping out unfinished components for extensive adjustment on the construction site.For especially complicated projects, the team is able to bring the actual environment of the staircase into the workshop. Full height temporary walls are constructed to the same radius and footprint as the actual stairwell. The complete helical stair for the Newport residence was preassembled in the shop and trucked to the property. This enabled the craftsmen to identify potential problems and check that the components fitted together before installation. And the result is a brilliant example of how historic craftsmanship does not necessarily mean something from the past. Mortises and wedges, a time-honored woodworking method, can be adapted to modern construction through CAD modeling, CNC machinery and precise hand-fitting, maintaining the character of a historic American home.Images Courtesy: Markrichey
Article Summary: The helical staircase is being built for the restoration of a historic home in Newport, Rhode Island. It is a Mark Richey Woodworking’s design and a revival of a late 16th century European method of building stairs. The technique originated in the construction of European staircases in the late 1500s, when wealthy homes and castles had elaborate staircases.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
